title: MC0-08331
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Romania.
As a Roma, he fears persecution by the Romanian authorities and society if he were to return to Romania.

He is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. He asserts that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility. He also argues that the RPD erred in concluding that the discrimination he would face upon retuning to Romania does not cumulatively amount to persecution.

For the reasons set out below, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) concludes that the RPD erred in its assessment of the appellant's credibility and in its analysis of what constitutes persecution. After analyzing all the evidence, the RAD concludes that the appellant has established a serious possibility of persecution in Romania and that he is a Convention refugee.
The appeal is allowed.
The RAD applied the standard of correctness.1 The RAD conducted an independent review of the evidence.

It is important to note that the appellant is not challenging the RPD's conclusion that he did not present any evidence to establish the possibility of persecution by reason of his being a Pentecostal Christian. The RAD conducted an independent analysis and sees no error with this conclusion.

The appellant, however, is contesting the RPD's credibility findings. He argues that the RPD failed to consider his explanation that he has no education. He is also contesting the RPD's conclusion that he has allegedly failed to cumulatively establish a serious possibility of persecution in Romania because he is Roma.

With respect, as set out below, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD erred in concluding that there were serious contradictions and inconsistencies in the appellant's written account, undermining his credibility. The RAD also concludes that the RPD erred in its analysis of what constitutes persecution.

After analyzing all the evidence, the RAD concludes that the appellant has established a serious possibility of persecution in Romania because of his particular profile, namely that he is Roma, uneducated and not socially integrated in Romania and that he and his wife were the victims of physical assault. The Refugee Protection Division erred in its assessment of the appellant's credibility Omission in the testimony

The RAD concludes that the RPD erred in drawing an adverse credibility inference based on the appellant's testimony that his problems began in 1994, when his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form)2 indicates that his problems began well before 1994.

It is true that when asked about his problems in Romania, the appellant spontaneously mentioned the 1994 incident in which he was harassed by his co-workers after finding a stable job XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.3 The latter concealed his work tools, which led to charges of theft being laid against him. Because he refused to admit to having committed the thefts, the police beat him. When asked if there were any other reasons why he left Romania, the appellant replied that there were not.4 However, when asked immediately thereafter about the existence of problems before 1994, the appellant explained that he did not have the right to go to school. Consequently, he does not know how to read or write, which considerably limits his employment opportunities in Romania. He also explained that Roma are rejected by Romanians and that the latter tell them that they have no work for them.5 Although this is an adjustment in testimony, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant's testimony, taken as a whole, is consistent and not contradictory. It is clear from his testimony that it was because of the incidents in 1994 that he made the decision to leave Romania to apply for asylum in France. In his BOC Form,6 he clearly explains that before 1994 he dreamed of a stable, well-paying job in Romania. He did not want to live in poverty like his parents. It was thanks to a friend that he got the job as XXXX XXXX XXXX. However, that experience led to harassment by co-workers and physical assaults by police officers. Considering that this is a central element of his account, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD erred in drawing an adverse credibility inference because of the adjustment in testimony. Asylum application rejected in France

The RAD concludes that the RPD erred in concluding that if the appellant had proven that he was beaten on multiple occasions by the police in Romania and deprived of an education because he is Roma, France, being a signatory of the Refugee Convention, would have accepted his application for asylum submitted in 1994.

With all due respect, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD's decision is speculative. Case law states that an administrative tribunal can only make conclusions on implausibility in the clearest of cases.7 The RAD is of the opinion that in the absence of more information as to why the French authorities rejected the asylum application, it is not evident that if the appellant's application for asylum was rejected, it was because he was not credible with respect to the problems he would have encountered in Romania. The RAD is of the opinion that there is insufficient evidence to draw inferences based on the French authorities' rejection of the asylum application more than 25 years ago.

The RAD therefore concludes that the RPD erred in drawing an adverse credibility finding from the fact that the appellant was not granted asylum in France. Contradiction regarding the most recent return to Romania

The RAD concludes that the RPD did not err in drawing an adverse credibility finding based on contradictions between the appellant's testimony and his refugee protection claim form8 with regard to his most recent stay in Romania.

The RAD agrees with the RPD. The fact that the appellant did not go to school in itself does not explain the contradiction as to whether he spent only one month in Romania9 or more than a year before coming to Canada in 2018.10

Moreover, in his forms, the RAD notes that the appellant even indicated that he worked as a XXXX XXXX between 2016 and 2018. However, according to his testimony, he returned to Romania only to renew his passport.11 The RAD is of the opinion that it is not simply a matter of remembering or not remembering dates. The RAD is of the opinion that, despite the fact that he did not go to school, the appellant should remember whether he worked as a XXXX XXXX for two years in Romania or whether he returned only to obtain his passport.
Consequently, in the absence of a satisfactory explanation, the RPD was correct in concluding that the appellant returned to Romania in 2016, as he stated on his refugee claim forms.
However, the RAD accepts, as the RPD noted, that the appellant did not mention any incidents subsequent to his return to Romania in 2016.

It is nonetheless important to determine whether or not, in light of the allegations found to be credible and the appellant's profile, the RPD's conclusion as to what constitutes persecution is correct. The Refugee Protection Division erred in its analysis of what constitutes persecution
The RAD concludes that the RPD erred in concluding that the discrimination experienced by the appellant does not amount to persecution.

The appellant asserts that the various discriminatory measures to which he was subjected amount, cumulatively, to persecution. He asserts that the RPD carried out in an incomplete analysis and demonstrated a lack of knowledge of the documentary evidence regarding the treatment of Roma in Romania.

Paragraph 54 of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status12 states that: Differences in the treatment of various groups do indeed exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. Persons who receive less favourable treatment as a result of such differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution. This would be so if measures of discrimination lead to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature for the person concerned, e.g. serious restrictions on his right to earn his livelihood, his right to practise his religion, or his access to normally available educational facilities.

According to case law, persecution can be concluded to exist when a person is relentlessly tormented through cruel treatment or when there is a succession of measures taken systematically in order to punish.13 For discriminatory acts to constitute persecution, they must be "sufficiently serious and occur over such a long period of time that it can be said that the claimants' physical or moral integrity is threatened."14

In concluding that the appellant had not established a serious possibility of persecution, the RPD considered that the appellant's wife and children were not living on the street in Romania, that the children were attending school, that he had travelled throughout Romania to work as a XXXX XXXX, that he could travel freely to any country in Europe and that, according to the documentary evidence, instances of police brutality occurred in limited cases.15
The RAD does not agree with the appellant's arguments that the RPD erred in concluding that his children attend school. According to his refugee protection claim forms, his children are students.16
However, with respect, the RAD accepts the appellant's argument that the RPD's analysis is incomplete.

The RAD is of the opinion that the RPD should have considered the documentary evidence more closely to question whether Romanian authorities are creating an atmosphere of intolerance in the country.17

The RAD nonetheless notes that the documentary evidence available to the RPD at the time of its decision, which is still available in the most recent version of the National Documentation Package on Romania, indicated that sources have reported that some government officials make discriminatory remarks about Roma and that the Romanian president reportedly stated that many nomadic Roma traditionally live by theft.18 The same evidence also reveals that Roma are subjected to racist media and political campaigns, including ethnic profiling, on a daily basis; that anti-Roma signs, slogans and songs are [translation] "common and widespread," in particular at widely televised sporting events; and that discriminatory advertising messages are featured in print publications and on the Internet.
More recent evidence reveals that government officials have publicly singled out Roma as being responsible for the spread of COVID-19 in the country.19
In light of the evidence, the RAD concludes that the Romanian authorities maintain an atmosphere of intolerance towards Roma.

The RAD is also of the opinion that the RPD should have considered the 2012 incident in which the appellant's then-pregnant wife was beaten by a shopkeeper without anyone intervening. In the RAD's view, it is necessary to ask whether, in light of the objective documentary evidence, assaults on Roma by ordinary citizens in Romania are frequent and, if so, whether they can obtain adequate state protection.

According to the documentary evidence available at the time of the RPD's decision, one source stated that [translation] "the pervasiveness of racism and racially motivated violence continues to alienate many Roma families and groups from mainstream society."20

As for the treatment by the authorities and the protection available, the RAD notes that the document that the RPD relied on mentions that one source stated that relations between the Romanian authorities and Roma have improved since 1990.21 However, the same document quotes another source as mentioning that, over the last three to four years, physical assaults by police officers on Roma in Races [translation] "seemed to be frequent and gratuitous," and that more than 40 people were beaten and that some of the victims filed complaints with the police but that all the complaints were dismissed. The RPD erred in failing to mention this conflicting evidence in its reasons and by failing to explain why it preferred the source alleging that relations had improved.
The RAD is also of the opinion that the RPD should have demonstrated in its reasons that it took into consideration the very precarious nature of the appellant's employment.
The RAD considered the appellant's allegations found to be credible.

The appellant has been deprived of education since childhood because he is Roma. This has had an impact on his employability. He is unable to read or write. Despite his desire to find a stable job, due to discrimination against Roma, the appellant has mostly held precarious employment that required him to travel throughout Romania to support himself and his family. When he found a stable job generally held by Romanians and not by Roma, he was harassed by this co-workers, accused of theft and beaten by the police. After failing to obtain protection in France, the appellant returned to Romania in 1996. He was intercepted by the police and beaten. In 2012, when his wife was pregnant, she was beaten by a merchant because her two-year-old daughter was crying. No one intervened to help her. The appellant and his wife and children then headed to France where they lived as nomads, because they were constantly being chased by the French police. They returned to Romania afterwards.
The RAD considers that the appellant had access to identity documents and does not claim that he had problems accessing health care or problems accessing housing in Romania.

However, the RAD considers that the various problems the appellant experienced are sufficiently serious and occurred over a sufficiently long period of time to conclude that his psychological integrity was threatened.
The RAD is of the opinion that the problems the appellant described lead to the conclusion that the discrimination he experienced in Romania cumulatively amounts to persecution.
Furthermore, in light of the recent objective evidence, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant demonstrated a prospective risk should he return to Romania.

Recent evidence reveals that police are raiding Roma communities and forcibly evicting them.22 Roma are still discriminated against in the area of employment. Employers refuse to hire them. The recent evidence also indicates that police harassment and police brutality towards Roma are still a problem. The appellant has rebutted the presumption of state protection
According to the recent documentary evidence, impunity for those responsible for certain human rights violations is a problem in Romania.23

According to a report by the Special Rapporteur of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the system for handling complaints of police abuse is cumbersome, complex and inefficient, making abuse easy and making accountability the exception rather than the norm.24
As noted above, the appellant is credible in his allegations of persecution by the police.

As for discrimination against Roma, the evidence shows that, although the law prohibits discrimination based on ethnicity, the government does not effectively enforce these prohibitions, and Roma often experience discrimination and violence.25

In light of the foregoing, the RAD concludes that the appellant has demonstrated that he would not be able to receive adequate state protection in Romania. In the RAD's view, he has rebutted the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
The RAD also considered the possibility of an internal flight alternative in Romania. The Refugee Protection Division concludes that no viable internal flight alternative exists for the appellant

Considering the appellant's particular profile, the RAD concludes that he would not be safe from persecution anywhere in Romania. After analyzing the documentary evidence,26 the RAD concludes that the treatment of Roma, particularly those without an education, is the same everywhere in Romania.

In light of the above, the RAD concludes that the RPD erred. Based on the RAD's analysis of the merits of the claim, the RAD exercises its powers pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, sets aside the RPD's determination and substitutes the determination that should have been made.

The RAD concludes that the appellant has established a serious possibility of persecution on one of the five Convention grounds, namely on racial grounds, by reason of his belonging to the Roma minority.

The appeal is allowed. The RAD substitutes its own determination that the appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a Convention refugee.
